records.question: According to the Introduction, how did corals from the thermally variable pool compare to corals from the thermally moderate pool in terms of mortality and photochemical efficiency?
records.ground_truth_answer: Corals from the thermally variable pool showed lower mortality and less severe declines in photochemical efficiency than corals from the thermally moderate pool; all corals from the variable pool hosted heat-resistant symbionts.
ground_truth_chunks: The most variable of these pools reaches 34–35C during summer low tides and shows a daily temperature range of as much as 6C.

We show that corals from the thermally variable pool, all of which hosted heat-resistant symbionts, show lower mortality and less severe declines in photochemical efficiency than corals from the thermally moderate pool, regardless of symbiont type.

records.question: What statistical method was used to analyze the mortality data, and how were survivors handled?
records.ground_truth_answer: Mortality was analyzed using Cox proportional hazards regression (as implemented in R), with individuals that survived to the end of the experimental period treated as censored.
ground_truth_chunks: To analyze the mortality data, we used Cox proportional hazards regression as implemented in R (Crawley [2007](#page-10-0)), with censoring of individuals that survived to the end of the experimental period.
We used a multifactor model, with (1) experimental run, (2) temperature treatment, and (3) the treatment by experimental group interaction as factors.

records.question: According to the Discussion, what two factors likely contributed to the unusually low mortalities in corals from the smaller pool?
records.ground_truth_answer: They hosted the high temperature-resistant Symbiodinium D, and they had survived either selection or acclimatization to their native, thermally variable pool.
ground_truth_chunks: Our experimental results show that the corals naturally growing in a thermally variable lagoon pool resisted heat stress, while those corals from a larger, more moderate pool suffered high mortalities, regardless of their Symbiodinium type.

The unusually low mortalities seen in the smaller pool's corals are likely due to at least two simultaneous factors. First, all the corals in the smaller pool hosted the high temperature-resistant Symbiodinium D (Rowan [2004;](#page-10-0) Berkelmans and van Oppen [2006\)](#page-9-0), and second, they all had survived either selection or acclimatization to their native, thermally variable pool.
